summary: I read src/server.mjs, src/store.mjs, test/notes.test.mjs, test/helpers.mjs and src/client.mjs in full, and grepped for createStore/save/remove callers. All 7 tests pass, but I reproduced a crash on Node 24: a POST whose save() fails takes the whole process down, because the rejection is never awaited or caught.

findings.issue: The async save() is fire-and-forget, so the handler's try/catch never sees its rejection. If the write fails (missing directory, EACCES, disk full, file locked on Windows), the rejection is unhandled and Node 15+ exits the process. I reproduced this with NOTES_FILE pointing into a directory that does not exist: the POST died with ENOENT and exit code 1, and no response was sent. This breaks the house rule that a bad request returns a 4xx/5xx JSON error and never crashes the server. The same line also sends 201 before anything is on disk, so a client can be told a note was saved when it was not.
findings.fix: Use `await store.save()` before sending the response, so a failure goes through the existing catch and returns a 500 JSON error. Also decide whether a failed save should roll back the in-memory note (notes.delete(note.id)) so memory and disk do not drift.

findings.issue: The write is not atomic and nothing serializes it. Two POSTs close together start overlapping writeFile calls on the same path, which the Node docs say is unsafe: the writes can interleave, or an older snapshot can land after a newer one. A crash mid-write leaves a truncated file. Either way the file on disk can end up corrupt or stale.
findings.fix: Chain saves through one promise so only one write runs at a time, e.g. `let pending = Promise.resolve(); save = () => (pending = pending.then(write, write))`. Write to `${file}.tmp` and then `rename` it over `file` so each replacement is atomic.

findings.issue: An empty, truncated or corrupt NOTES_FILE (which the non-atomic write above can produce) makes JSON.parse throw inside createStore, so the server cannot start, with no message naming the file. Valid JSON that is not an array throws a TypeError in for..of. Any non-numeric id makes Math.max return NaN, so every later note gets the id 'NaN' and they overwrite each other in the Map. Spreading every key into Math.max also hits a RangeError once the store gets very large.
findings.fix: Wrap the load in try/catch and rethrow with the file path in the message (or refuse to start with a clear error). Check that the parsed value is an array. Compute nextId with a reduce that skips non-integer ids, e.g. `let max = 0; for (const id of notes.keys()) { const n = Number(id); if (Number.isInteger(n) && n > max) max = n }`.

findings.code: test('notes survive a restart when a file is set', async () => {
findings.issue: The new test only calls the store directly. Nothing tests the server-side change: POST /notes persisting through HTTP, the NOTES_FILE wiring, or a failed save. That missing test is exactly how the crash at server.mjs:46 got through. The house rule is that every behavior change comes with a test. The test also leaves its temp directory behind.
findings.fix: Add an HTTP-level test: start createApp(createStore({ file })), POST a note, then build a new store from the same file and check the note is there. Add a test where save fails (file inside a directory that does not exist) and assert the POST returns a 5xx JSON error and the server still answers GET /notes. Remove the temp directory with rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true }) in a finally block.

findings.issue: Now that the store persists, remove() only changes memory. No route calls it yet, but a future DELETE route that forgets to call save() would bring deleted notes back after a restart. Only create() is paired with a save.
findings.fix: Document that callers must call save() after any change, or make save part of create/remove in the store so persistence cannot be skipped.
